objections.trigger: Assisting or even being present at a suicide should be a crime — it deters, and it refuses complicity in a grave act.
objections.diagnosis: Criminalizing assistance and presence does not prevent the sovereign exit — it manufactures the solitary, more violent death its proponents lament, and the obstruction is wrong on sovereignty before any consequence is counted.

responses.short: This objection is self-refuting on its own aim. Criminalizing assistance and presence does not stop the sovereign exit — it strips it of company and forces it toward more solitary, more violent means, so a present loved one isn't prosecuted. The regime that claims to protect against a lonely, brutal death is the thing that manufactures it. And the obstruction was wrong on sovereignty before the backfire was even counted.
responses.medium: The criminalization case is the obstruction charge made concrete, and it collapses under its own stated purpose. The argument for punishing those who assist or are merely present is that it deters and marks the act as grave. But it does not deter the determined sovereign agent; it only determines the conditions under which they go. Drive assistance and witness under threat of prosecution and you do not get fewer exits — you get lonelier ones, undertaken in secret, by harsher means chosen precisely because they need no accomplice and leave no one exposed. The objection that elsewhere laments the person 'dying alone' is, in this form, the direct cause of their dying alone: it makes the presence of a companion a crime. So the regime fails twice over. It fails consequentially, producing the isolation and brutality it purports to prevent and forfeiting the very deliberation and farewell that the survivor-grief objection claims to want. And it fails at the root, because even a criminalization scheme that somehow worked would still be obstructing a sovereign exit — wrong on sovereignty before any of its effects are tallied. The backfire is the vivid part; the sovereignty violation is the load-bearing part.
responses.long:
Of all the objections in this family, this is the one whose obstruction is least abstract, because it asks for an actual coercive apparatus — the criminalization of assisting, or even being present at, a death. Its proponents do not merely disapprove; they want the law to punish the companion. Meeting it well means taking both its arms: the consequentialist case for the regime, and the deeper question of whether the obstruction would be legitimate even if the regime worked.

Start with the regime's own logic, because it is where the objection is weakest and does not know it. The case for criminalizing assistance and presence rests on two claims: that it deters the act, and that it expresses the gravity of the act by refusing complicity. Take deterrence first. The sovereign, determined agent is not deterred by prosecuting the people around them — they are not the one being threatened. What the threat actually controls is not whether the exit happens but the conditions under which it happens. Make the presence of a companion prosecutable and you do not produce a living person; you produce a person who must go without a companion, in secret, by means chosen for requiring no accomplice and exposing no one. The regime does not subtract deaths from the world. It subtracts witnesses, deliberation, and care from the deaths that occur. And here the criminalization case runs directly into the objection that so often sits beside it — the lament that people should not 'die alone,' that the tragedy is the isolation and the violence. That lament, in this form, is self-inflicted: the law that criminalizes presence is the mechanism that enforces dying alone. It manufactures precisely the solitary, brutal death it claims to stand against, and it forecloses the very window for goodbye and reconsideration that the survivor-grief objection insists it wants to preserve. A regime that produces the harm it names as its reason is not a hard moral tradeoff; it is incoherent on its own terms.

The expressive arm fares no better. Marking the act as grave by punishing the companion does not express reverence for the dying person; it expresses a willingness to prosecute the one human being who refused to let them be alone. Whatever symbolic content that has, it is not on the side of the person the regime claims to protect.

Now the part that matters even if every empirical claim above were contested — the obstruction charge proper. Suppose an objector grants none of the backfire, or claims the deterrent works better than I allow. The criminalization regime is still obstructing a sovereign exit. It is wrong on sovereignty before a single consequence is counted, in exactly the way the other nodes establish: a competent agent's authority over their own life is not contingent on the state's approval of how, or whether, they end it, and turning their companions into criminals is simply obstruction conducted at one remove — coercing the exit by coercing everyone who might stand beside it. This is why the consequentialist collapse, vivid as it is, is not actually the foundation. The foundation is that the exit was the agent's to make, and the regime has no standing to forbid it however it dresses the forbidding. The backfire shows the regime is also stupid; the sovereignty point shows it is also wrong.

Residual, marked honestly. The consequentialist arm leans on empirical claims about what criminalization does to the manner of death — claims that are well-supported but contestable, and that are owed real documentation rather than assertion (the records that would carry them are an RWE matter, not yet attached). Strip that arm away entirely and the node still stands on its second leg, but that second leg is the same one the whole library rests on: that no one else holds the authority to conscript a person's continuation. An objector who denies that — who holds that the community may compel a person's continuation in the act's prevention — can accept every word about the backfire and still insist the obstruction is licensed, at which point the disagreement has relocated, as it always does, to that premise. The argument wins the coherence point outright and stakes the rest where everything here is staked.

objections.trigger: You can't give valid consent to dying when you're mentally ill — the illness is making the choice, so honoring it isn't respecting autonomy, it's abandoning someone to their disorder.
objections.diagnosis: The objection vaults from 'this condition can impair some decisions' to 'this person can validly decide nothing about their own life' — an overgeneralization capacity assessment is built to refuse; gating the exercise on assessed competence is the honest answer, abolishing the right is not.

responses.short: A diagnosis is not a global revocation of decisional standing. Capacity is decision-specific and assessable — that is why clinics assess it rather than reading it off a chart. The objection's leap is from 'illness can impair some choices' to 'this person may decide nothing,' and that leap is the error. Gate the exercise on assessed competence; do not abolish the right.
responses.medium: The objection's force depends on a slide between two very different claims. The defensible one: mental illness can impair decision-making, sometimes severely. The indefensible one it slides into: that a diagnosed person therefore cannot validly decide anything about their own continuation. Capacity does not work that way and clinical practice already knows it — capacity is assessed for a specific decision at a specific time, and people with serious psychiatric conditions routinely retain it for many grave decisions, including refusals of treatment that foreseeably end in death. So the honest structure is a gate, not a wall: a decision-specific competence threshold determines who may exercise the right, while the right itself remains. That is what 'gated access' means and why this is the node where gating is correct rather than a dodge. Now the deepest version of the objection, which deserves naming: not that the illness clouds the reasoning, but that it manufactures the very desire — that depression doesn't merely impair the choice, it authors it, so honoring the preference honors the disorder. This has real force, and only for some conditions, and it meets its limit at the same place the 'temporary' slogan does — the treatment-resistant case, where the desire has persisted through every attempt to lift the condition allegedly producing it. A preference that survives the exhaustion of treatment is no longer plausibly just the symptom speaking.
responses.long:
This is the hardest objection in the family and the one most easily mishandled in both directions — either by waving away a real worry or by surrendering an entire class of persons to a blanket disqualification. Both are failures. The argument has to hold a competence gate open while refusing a competence wall, and it has to engage the strongest form of the worry rather than the strawman.

Begin with what is true, because the objection earns a real concession and conceding it is what makes the rest credible. Mental illness can impair decision-making, sometimes profoundly; acute psychosis, severe cognitive distortion, states in which a person cannot retain or weigh the relevant considerations are real, and in such states the conditions for valid consent are genuinely absent. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the inference the objection draws from it: that because some psychiatric states defeat capacity, a diagnosed person as such cannot validly decide about their own continuation. That inference is an overgeneralization, and it is precisely the one that the entire practice of capacity assessment exists to refuse. Capacity is not a global property you have or lack by virtue of a label; it is decision-specific and time-specific — the ability to understand, retain, weigh, and communicate a choice about this matter, now. People with serious, chronic psychiatric conditions routinely retain capacity for grave decisions, including the legally recognized right to refuse life-sustaining treatment in full knowledge that refusal will kill them. We do not tell the competent patient with severe depression that their refusal of dialysis is 'the illness talking' and override it. The objection, applied consistently, would have to — and that exposes it as proving far too much.

So the honest structure is a gate, not a wall, and this is the node where that distinction is load-bearing. A decision-specific competence threshold determines who may exercise the right; the right itself is not contingent on the absence of all diagnosis. That is what gated access is for. It is not a hedge or a softening of the sovereignty claim — it is the sovereignty claim applied correctly to a population in which capacity genuinely varies. The 2b spine runs straight through it: where competence is present, obstruction is wrong on sovereignty, exactly as it is for any competent agent; where competence is absent, the conditions for an autonomous exit are not met and the question is different in kind. The objector who wants a wall has to deny that the competent psychiatric patient exists at all, and the assessment literature, and the ordinary law of treatment refusal, both say otherwise.

Now the strongest version, which a serious treatment of this cannot skip. The deepest objection is not that the illness clouds the reasoning around the choice; it is that the illness manufactures the choice — that depression does not merely impair deliberation but authors the very desire to die, so that a capacity assessment finding 'understands, retains, weighs, communicates' can be satisfied while the preference being assessed is itself the symptom. On this view, respecting the preference is not respecting autonomy; it is taking dictation from the disorder. This has genuine force and I will not pretend it dissolves. It has force for some conditions and not all, and it meets a hard limit at the same place the 'temporary problem' objection does: the treatment-resistant case. If the worry is that the desire is an artifact of a condition that treatment would lift, then the case where the condition has been subjected to every available treatment and has not lifted — and the desire has persisted across that whole arc — is the case where the 'it's just the symptom' story has run out of explanatory room. A preference that outlives the exhaustion of the treatments aimed at its alleged source is no longer plausibly reducible to that source. The value-distortion objection is strongest against the freshly-diagnosed, untreated, acute presentation, and weakest exactly where the right is most defensibly exercised — the durable, competent, treatment-resistant case. That is not a coincidence; it is the gate doing its work.

Two residuals, stated plainly. First, the gate is real, which means this node concedes more than the others: there are persons and states for whom the competence condition is not met and for whom an exit is not an autonomous one, and the argument does not claim sovereignty for them — it claims that their existence does not retract it from the competent. Second, the value-distortion worry does not vanish for the hard cases; it weakens, and reasonable people will disagree about how completely treatment-resistance answers it. The argument earns the competent, treatment-resistant case and the gating principle; it does not earn the claim that capacity assessment is infallible or that distortion is ever fully ruled out. And underneath all of it sits the same premise the whole library leans on — sovereignty over one's own life. Deny it and even a flawless competence finding licenses nothing. The gate is where this objection is honestly met; the premise is where, like every other, it is finally staked.

objections.trigger: Life is sacred and inviolable — ending it is wrong whatever the person wants, and society may step in to honor that inviolability.
objections.diagnosis: The argument leaps from 'life has (sacred) value' to 'others may forcibly preserve this life against its bearer' — a license that only follows if the sanctity binds the agent without their consent, i.e. as an external imposition on a sovereign body.

responses.short: Grant that life has value — even that it's sacred. The leap is from 'life is sacred' to 'others may forcibly preserve this life against its bearer.' That doesn't follow. To license obstruction, the sanctity has to bind the agent independent of their consent — which means imposing one party's metaphysics on a sovereign body. For the agent who doesn't share it, that's not reverence. It's coercion wearing reverence's clothes.
responses.medium: The sanctity objection borrows the same invalid step the 'selfish' charge does, with the creditor swapped out. There, the survivors were owed; here, the value — or God — is owed. Concede the premise at its strongest: suppose life genuinely carries intrinsic, even sacred, value. It still does not follow that third parties may enforce that value on the body of someone who rejects it. The claim that life is sacred and the claim that others may forcibly preserve a particular life against its bearer's will are different claims, and only the first has any independent plausibility. For the second to license obstruction, the agent must be bound by the sanctity whether or not they accept it — the value has to reach into a life from outside and override the person living it. That is exactly what a secular, or simply dissenting, agent denies. Honoring an inviolability the bearer does not hold is not protecting them from error; it is conscripting their body into the service of someone else's commitment. The objection cannot get from a value to a license without quietly assuming that its value is binding on people who never signed up for it.
responses.long:
This objection has an old and serious pedigree, and it is worth meeting on its strongest ground rather than the caricature. The strongest version is not a slogan about life being precious; it is the claim that life possesses intrinsic, perhaps sacred, value — value it has independent of whether its bearer recognizes it — and that this value grounds a duty of preservation binding on everyone, including third parties who may therefore act to prevent its destruction. Stated that fully, it is a real argument. It also contains a seam, and the seam is the same one that runs through the obstruction charge generally.

Concede the front half. Suppose life does carry intrinsic value, even sacredness — grant the objector their richest metaphysics of worth. The question is what follows for third parties. The inference the objection needs is: life is sacred, therefore others may forcibly preserve a given life against the will of the one living it. That inference is invalid, and the reason is structural. Having value and being subject to others' coercive preservation are not the same status. A great many things carry genuine value without thereby licensing strangers to seize and protect them against the wishes of the person whose value it is; the value of a life, in particular, is realized through the agent living it, not stored in a vault others may guard over the agent's objection. To move from the sacredness of life to a license to obstruct, the objector has to add a premise: that the sanctity binds the agent regardless of the agent's own commitments — that it reaches into the life from outside and overrides the person whose life it is. And that added premise is precisely what the dissenting agent rejects.

This is the obstruction charge in its purest external-imposition form, and it survives an objector who has abandoned the entire debt-and-compensation framing, because it never used that framing. The survivors-are-owed story does not appear; the agent owes no one anything in this version. The only thing being asserted is a value, and the only thing being claimed from it is a license to coerce. The 2b spine cuts straight through: an agent sovereign over their own life cannot be conscripted into honoring a sanctity they do not hold, on their own body, by parties who do hold it. Reverence enforced on the unwilling is not reverence; it is the use of another person's body as the site where someone else's metaphysics gets vindicated. The sanctity may be real to the one who believes it. It does not thereby become binding on the one who does not, and a pluralist order — one that does not let any single account of the sacred command the bodies of those outside it — has to say so.

The residual is sharp and I will not soften it, because it is where the committed objector actually lives. Suppose the sanctity is not merely sincerely held but objectively true and binding on all rational agents whether or not they assent — strong theistic or natural-law realism, on which the duty of preservation is as real for the unbeliever as the law of gravity. On that view the agent IS bound, their dissent is simply error, and obstruction could be the enforcement of a duty they genuinely have. The argument does not refute that metaphysics; nothing short of a full engagement with the realism could. What it does is force the cost into the open: to license obstruction, the objector must claim not only that their account of the sacred is correct, but that its correctness entitles them to override a sovereign agent's authority over their own body and compel continuation on the strength of a value that agent rejects. Some will affirm exactly that. Most pluralists, asked whether one contested account of the sacred should command the bodies of everyone outside it, will not — and that refusal is the whole of what this rebuttal needs. The premise it finally rests on is, again, sovereignty over one's own life; deny it and the external value walks back in.

objections.trigger: Suicide is selfish — it dumps unbearable pain on the people left behind, who never consented to that grief.
objections.diagnosis: The charge conflates a debt owed to others with a license to conscript the agent's continuation — but a debt grounds a claim against the agent, never the right to imprison them.

responses.short: Grant the debt — assume you owe your survivors everything the objection claims. It still doesn't follow that they may forcibly keep you alive. A debt grounds a claim against you; it never grounds authority to conscript your continued existence. 'Selfish' scores the ledger — it says nothing about who holds the key to the cell, and no debt installs anyone as the warden.
responses.medium: The objection runs two claims together and the rebuttal only needs the seam. Claim one is descriptive: a death inflicts grief on survivors who didn't consent to it. Concede it entirely — it's often true. Claim two is the smuggled inference: that this uncompensated harm licenses others to obstruct the exit. That inference is invalid. We recognize debts everywhere — to creditors, dependents, the people who love us — and none of them convert into a standing to conscript the debtor: to commandeer a body and run it against the person's own will. A parent who abandons a child owes that child; the child does not thereby acquire the right to chain the parent to the house. The selfishness charge, even if it lands, scores a moral ledger — it cannot also conscript the debtor into staying alive. And note what the charge inverts: it weighs an agent's entire remaining life — every hour they would have to live inside the suffering — against the discomfort their absence causes others, and rules the others' discomfort decisive. That is the selfishness, relocated.
responses.long:
Take the objection at its strongest. Don't dispute the grief; assume it's severe, foreseeable, and uncompensated — that the survivors are genuinely harmed and genuinely did not consent. The objection's whole force is supposed to flow from that. It doesn't, and seeing why isolates the one thing this rebuttal actually rests on.

There are two propositions doing work. The first is a fact about consequences: an exit injures the people left behind. The second is a normative claim: that this injury makes the exit something others may rightfully prevent. The move from the first to the second is where the argument lives, and it is a non sequitur. Owing something to a person is not the same as that person holding authority to conscript you. We hold debts of every kind — financial, relational, the diffuse debt of being loved and depended upon — and not one of them licenses the creditor to take physical control of the debtor and compel the body to keep running against its will. The deadbeat parent owes the child; the child does not acquire a right to imprison the parent. The defaulting borrower owes the lender; the lender does not get to extract labor by force. The structure is identical here: even a real, grave, uncompensated debt to survivors generates a claim against the agent — moral pressure, an obligation to consider, to soften, to say goodbye — never a license for the survivors, or the state acting in their name, to conscript the agent's continuation: to hold the body shut and compel it to keep living for them.

This is the obstruction charge, and it is built to survive an objector who rejects the entire surrounding apparatus of compensation. Someone can deny that exit is permissible, deny that the agent has compensated anyone, deny the whole debt-and-balance framing — and the rebuttal still stands, because it never needed that framing. It needs one premise, and a thin one: that no one else holds standing authority to conscript a person's continuation — that the body running someone's suffering may not be commandeered to keep running for the people around them. Grant that, and obstruction is wrong on its face, debt or no debt. And notice what this premise does not require: it does not require that a person "owns" themselves, that a life is a possession or a holding of any kind. It asks only that a power be denied — the power to compel another's continued existence — and that denial is available even to someone who rejects all talk of owning persons outright.

That single premise — that no one holds standing authority to conscript another's continuation — is also the only place this argument can be attacked, and honesty requires naming it. The serious objector does not re-press the grief; they assert the contrary power. They hold that others may, in the relevant sense, keep you to your continuation: that a life is constituted by the relationships that made it, woven through with people who have a stake in its going on, and that this stake can compel you to remain. This is the communitarian and the theistic move, and it is not stupid — it points at something real about how lives are embedded. But notice the cost of taking it seriously enough to license obstruction: it entails that the people around you hold a standing veto over the continuation of your existence — that you may be compelled to remain alive inside unbearable suffering because others have an interest in your staying. State that conclusion plainly and most people who reach for "selfish" recoil from it, because stated plainly it is conscription: a person held to a life they are trying to leave, for the benefit of those who want them in it. The charge was meant to express that the agent weighs too lightly the harm to others. The rebuttal returns the weighing: an objection that resolves a person's entire remaining lifetime of suffering against the grief their absence would cause, and decides for the grief, has not corrected a selfishness — it has performed one, conscripting the agent's continuation to the comfort of others.

The residual is exact and I won't paper over it. If others genuinely do hold that authority — if a person's continuation really is something the community may compel for its own sake — then the obstruction charge gets traction and this rebuttal weakens with it. The argument does not defeat that claim; it forces the objector to assert it nakedly, and to own its shape: that an interest in your company can compel your continuation, which is to say it can conscript it. Most won't. That is where the load sits — and it sits there without ever requiring a person to be their own property, which is the whole point of running the spine this way.

objections.trigger: Suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem — whatever's driving it will pass, and then the irreversible choice is made on a feeling that would have lifted.
objections.diagnosis: The slogan smuggles a universal ('all such problems are temporary') that is empirically false for intractable cases, and even where reversibility is uncertain it conflates the authority to choose with a guarantee of the outcome.

responses.short: "It's temporary" is two claims. *Your* suffering will remit is unknowable in advance and the chooser's call, not the objector's. *Because remission is sometimes possible, no one may have the option* is the objection to the right — and it does not follow. Concede the empirics whole: remission is real, common, and no one's suffering is asserted permanent. The bar still requires a premise the objector never defends — that preventing every death that would have remitted is worth prolonging, against the person's will, every case that will not. That is a trade-off between two populations whose costs fall on different people, decided under uncertainty no one escapes. Irreversibility licenses safeguards; it does not license deleting the option. Prohibition only systematizes the other error — and hides it.
responses.medium:
"It's temporary" does two different jobs. Applied to a person — *your* suffering will remit — it is a claim no one can know in advance, and whether to act under that uncertainty is the chooser's, not the objector's. Applied as a categorical bar — *because remission is sometimes possible, no one may have the option* — it is the objection to the right, and it fails.

Concede the empirics in full: remission is real, common, sometimes spontaneous, and the rebuttal asserts that no one's suffering is permanent. The bar still does not follow. "Remission is sometimes possible" reaches "remove the option for all" only across a premise the objector never defends — that preventing every false-positive exit (a death that would have remitted) is worth imposing every false-negative imprisonment (suffering that will not remit, prolonged against the sufferer's will). That is a contested trade-off between two populations, not a fact about remission.

And the costs fall on different parties. “It might improve” is not knowledge the objector holds — it is the condition of every decision, the clinician's included. Nor is the asymmetry of rationality the objection quietly assumes — exit as the distorted wish, continuation as the clear one — real: optimism bias and the projection that one's present endurance will hold distort the case for staying as surely as despair distorts the case for going. Neither side is the lucid baseline; granting the symmetry does not make exit rational or continuation irrational, only removes the objector's claim to the sole clear head. The live question is who decides, under irreducible uncertainty and distortion, when the two errors are asymmetric. Irreducibility legitimates *safeguards* — capacity assessment, waiting periods — but safeguards calibrate the decision; the categorical bar deletes it. The objector trades on the slide from "should be hard" to "should be unavailable." And prohibition is not the costless baseline it pretends to be: it institutionalizes the false negatives and drives the determined to unregulated deaths. Every regime picks which error to systematize, and who holds the call.
responses.long:
The objection conflates two claims and survives only by the equivocation. Disambiguated:

- (A) Applied to a person — "your suffering specifically will remit." A claim about one case, which neither the objector nor anyone else can know ex ante, and which this library does not adjudicate: whether to act under irreducible uncertainty about one's own future is the chooser's call, not the objector's.
- (B) Applied as a categorical bar — "because remission is sometimes possible, the option must be unavailable to everyone." A claim about institutions, made on behalf of no one in particular. This is the objection to the right, and it fails.

It fails because the empirical premise does not entail the conclusion. Concede the premise in full — remission is real, frequent, sometimes spontaneous; the recoverable class is large; the perception of permanence is itself often a remitting symptom. None of this is contested, and the rebuttal asserts that no one's suffering is permanent. Grant all of it. The bar still does not follow, because "remission is sometimes possible" reaches "remove the option for all" only across a bridging premise the objector never states and never defends: that preventing every false-positive exit (a death that would have remitted) is worth imposing every false-negative imprisonment (suffering that will not remit, prolonged against the sufferer's will). That is a contestable trade-off between two populations of bad outcomes — not a fact about remission. Stated plainly, few would endorse it; smuggled inside "but it's temporary," it passes unexamined. Naming it is most of the work.

Three pressures finish it:

1. The symmetry runs deeper than uncertainty, and so does the objector's evasion. Start with the uncertainty: “it might improve” is not privileged knowledge the objector holds — it is the shared condition of every consequential decision, the clinician's “keep trying” included. But beneath the empirical claim sits an asymmetry of rationality the objection leans on without ever stating it: that the wish to exit is the distorted judgment — depression talking, the perception of permanence that is itself a remitting symptom — while the pull to continue is the clear-eyed one. That asymmetry is false, and naming it is the amplifier the bare error-cost point leaves implicit. Both judgments run under bias. The very optimism the objection invokes — “it will get better” — is itself a documented distortion: optimism bias, the planning fallacy, the projection bias that assumes one's present capacity to endure will simply hold, the status-quo and sunk-cost pulls that inflate the standing case for staying. The mind reaching toward exit is not uniquely compromised; the mind insisting on continuation is not uniquely lucid. And the guardrail matters precisely here: grant that both sides decide under irreducible distortion and the objector's privileged vantage evaporates — which does not make continuation irrational, and does not make exit the rational default. It makes neither the clean baseline. It returns the question to exactly where it already was: who decides, under irreducible uncertainty and irreducible distortion, when the two errors are radically asymmetric and fall on different parties. The objector wants to bear none of the cost of being wrong, and to claim the sole clear head while doing it, all while removing the decision from the one person who bears all of it.

2. Generalized, the objector's principle proves far too much. "Possible future improvement licenses overriding present autonomous refusal" would compel people to remain in marriages, to undergo refused treatment — any irreversible high-stakes choice where waiting might help. We accept this nowhere else at comparable stakes. The honest asymmetry: irreversibility here is genuinely higher, and that legitimates safeguards — capacity assessment, waiting periods, screening for pressure. But safeguards calibrate the decision; the categorical bar deletes it. The objector trades on the conflation of "should be hard and scrutinized" with "should be unavailable."

3. Prohibition is not the costless baseline it pretends to be. There is no error-free regime. A permissive regime produces false positives — people who would have remitted, gone; the rebuttal does not conjure them away. But prohibition institutionalizes the false negatives — suffering that will not remit, prolonged against the person's will — and drives the determined to violent, unregulated, terrifying deaths a regulated option would not. Every regime selects which error to systematize and who holds the call. Pretending prohibition systematizes none is the objector's sleight.

objections.trigger: Permit it and the option becomes a weapon against the weak — the elderly and disabled pressured, made to feel a burden, eased toward a door they never wanted; open it and you license atrocity, so it must stay shut for everyone.
keywords: right to die becomes duty to die
objections.diagnosis: The objection treats coerced deaths under a permissive regime as decisive while ignoring that prohibition neither eliminates coercion nor escapes the symmetric error of forcing the freely-decided to continue — it abolishes the liberty to avoid policing the abuse, a move made against no other abusable liberty.

responses.short: Coercion is two claims. *Permissive regimes produce pressured requests* is real — concede it whole. *Therefore bar the option for everyone* is the objection to the right, and it does not follow. Sharpen the premise to its strongest: the coerced death is the *categorically worse* error — death *and* injustice, beyond undoing — so the asymmetry runs against permission. Grant it whole; it still argues for *proportioning the safeguard to the worse error*, not for prohibition, because prohibition does not reduce that error. Coerced elderly death happens now, under prohibition — neglect, withdrawal, the unexamined "accident," no assessor in the room — the same irreversible harm, only unseen. Every liberty is abusable against the vulnerable; we police the abuse and protect the exposed, we do not abolish the liberty — unless no safeguard can contain it, which is asserted and never shown. Prohibition only systematizes the other error, and deletes the place you would catch it.
responses.medium:
Coercion's bite is not that death harms the decedent — it is the autonomy override: pressure manufactures a "choice" that frustrates a settled preference to live, and a coerced death is bad *for the person*. So set aside the reply that death is a non-bad event; it answers the wrong sub-objection. Answer instead on error distribution across regimes, and concede the empirical signal whole — permissive systems do generate burden- and capture-driven requests, and the disability-rights critique is owed a serious hearing.

The objector's strongest form denies the trade is symmetric: a coerced death stacks two irreversible harms — death *and* a manufactured choice — while forcing continuation is one harm and *reversible*, so the worse error sits on the permission side. Two answers. First, the asymmetry is not clean: forcing the *freely-decided* to continue is also two harms — the unwanted years, which cannot be un-suffered, *and* the injustice of overriding a settled choice — and for the determined it produces the violent unregulated death, death and injustice again. Second, and decisively: grant that the coerced death *is* the worse error, and it still argues for *proportioning the safeguard to the stakes*, not abolition — unless prohibition reduces that error. It does not. It relocates it into the dark: coerced elderly death occurs now as neglect, withdrawal, the unexamined "accident," with no assessor in the room. Prohibition does not abolish coercion; it abolishes the *checkpoint*. So the irreversibility the objector invokes cuts the other way — the worst error happens under prohibition too, unseen.

The objection also conflates two failures. *Acute* coercion — a pressuring heir, a family deciding for the patient — is procedure-addressable, more tractably than predicting remission: interview the person alone, screen for undue influence, impose cooling-off, require independent assessment. *Structural* coercion — the ambient "I am a burden," produced by underfunded elder care — is the genuine residual; procedure is weak because there is no one to screen out. But the honest conclusion is safeguards *and* provision: bundle the option with funded care, palliative access, real alternatives to weigh against the exit. Prohibition fixes neither the deprivation nor the burden-feeling; it removes one option and leaves every coercive condition standing.
responses.long:
Locate the bite first, because the obvious reply misses it. The temptation is to answer that death is a non-bad event for the one who dies — but coercion's force has nothing to do with whether death harms the decedent. Its force is the autonomy override: pressure manufactures a "decision" that frustrates a settled preference to live, so a coerced death is bad *for the person*. That granted, the real question is comparative — which regime, permission or prohibition, distributes irreducible error better. Concede the empirical signal whole: permissive regimes do generate burden- and capture-driven requests, and the disability-rights critique is owed a hearing, not a wave.

The objector's strongest move denies the trade is symmetric. The two errors are not the same size, it says: a coerced death stacks *two* irreversible harms — the death, and the injustice of a manufactured choice — while forcing continuation is a *single*, *reversible* harm. The person still lives; the suffering may remit; provision may yet come. So the asymmetry runs against permission, and the comparative frame collapses. Name it at full strength, because it is right that the errors differ. It is wrong about which way that cuts.

It is wrong first because the asymmetry is not clean. The "reversible single harm" reading holds only if the decision was never settled — which begs the question against the case the objection invokes, the *freely-decided* forced to continue. For that person, prohibition is also two harms: the substantive harm of an unwanted continuation, *and* the injustice of overriding a settled choice on behalf of no one in particular. Nor is it reversible as claimed: the interim years cannot be un-suffered, and reversing the outcome does not return the time. For the determined, prohibition produces the violent, unregulated death undertaken alone — death *and* injustice again. Both errors stack harm and injustice; the asymmetry is narrower than asserted.

Grant it anyway. Suppose the coerced death *is* the categorically worse error. That licenses building the safeguard *proportional to the stakes* — not closing the door. No liberty is revoked because its worst case is the worse one: property invites fraud, the franchise manipulation, contract the exploitation of the desperate, and in none do we abolish it for everyone. The objector's real reply is the disanalogy: those abuses are *recoverable* and death is not, so when the worst case is irreversible no imperfect safeguard is tolerable, and the rational answer just *is* prohibition. That reply hides one premise — that prohibition *reduces* the irreversible error. Pull it, and the disanalogy turns over.

Because prohibition does not reduce coerced death; it relocates it into the dark. Coerced elderly death needs no legal option to occur. It occurs now — neglect, withdrawal of care, the "accident" no one examines — and there it is *compounded by undetectability*: no assessor, no checkpoint, no review. Prohibition does not abolish coercion; it abolishes the one moment — an independent assessor, the person interviewed alone — where coercion can be named and refused. So the irreversibility the objector invoked cuts the other way: the irrecoverable coerced death happens under prohibition *too*, in greater number and unseen. The regulated regime does not manufacture the worst error; it manufactures the only scrutiny that catches it — and that scrutiny matters most exactly where the error is irreversible, because that is where a missed catch costs everything.

The objection also conflates two failures that come apart. *Acute* coercion — a pressuring heir, a family deciding for the patient — is procedure-addressable: catching a present party's undue influence beats predicting whether a depression will remit, so the safeguards are *more* credible here, not less. *Structural* coercion is the genuine residual — the ambient "I am a burden," produced not by any coercer but by underfunded elder care, where procedure is weak because there is no one to screen out. But its honest conclusion is *safeguards and provision*, not abolition: bundle the option with funded care, palliative access, a real life to weigh against the exit. Prohibition fixes neither; it deletes one option and leaves every coercive condition standing.

The residual stands unsanded, and the rebuttal says so: a permissive regime, however well-built, will produce coerced deaths its safeguards miss. The claim is only this — no error-free regime exists; prohibition's version of the *same* residual is both worse and invisible; and the greater irreversibility, fully granted, is met by *proportioning* the safeguard to it, not by denying the cost-bearer the decision. Coercion is a reason to build the safeguard well. It is not a reason to make the choice for everyone by making it for no one.

objections.trigger: Good palliative and hospice care can control suffering to the very end — terminal sedation reaches even the cases nothing else does. So no one truly *needs* assisted death; they are driven to it by gaps in care. Fund palliation properly and the demand dissolves. Permitting death just lets us avoid fixing what is actually broken.
objections.diagnosis: The objection treats palliation as a substitute for permission — assuming the request is exhaustively a demand for pain relief, so any relief a clinician can supply renders it moot — when 'manageable' is not 'acceptable to this person' and funding care and forbidding the choice are opposite levers, not the same one.

responses.short: A substitution argument that substitutes the wrong thing. Grant the clinical claim whole — palliation, up to terminal sedation, can blunt suffering to the end. It still does not reach *forbid the exit*, for two reasons. First, 'manageable' is not 'acceptable to this person': sedation into unconsciousness-until-death is the very mode of dying many requesters are declining, and offering it as proof their suffering is handled installs the clinician's threshold over the patient's — yet whose threshold governs a person's own death is the whole question, and it is the patient's. Second, even granting flawless palliative access, that is an argument to *fund palliation*, not to *prohibit the choice*: access and permission answer different questions, and the right regime runs both. 'Fix palliative care' and 'ban the exit' are opposite levers; the objection welds them only by assuming the exit was never more than a workaround for under-treatment — which begs the sovereignty question it has to win.
responses.medium:
The objection's strength is that it aims at the hardest case — the terminal, irremediable patient — and meets it with a genuine clinical fact: suffering can be controlled to the end, terminal sedation included. Take the fact at full value and the inference fails anyway.

Disambiguate first. *Applied to a person* — better care would relieve what is driving your request — it is a clinical claim about one case the library does not adjudicate. Whether the palliation on offer is acceptable to that patient is the patient's call; if it meets their need and they take it, nothing here says otherwise. *Applied as a categorical bar* — because palliation can manage suffering, the option must be closed to everyone — it is the objection to the right, and it fails.

It fails on a premise it never states: that the request is exhaustively about pain, so any relief a clinician can deliver is acceptable by definition. Both halves are false. 'Manageable' is not 'acceptable to this person.' The objection's trump card — sedation to the end — describes permanent oblivion until death, which is exactly the mode of dying many requesters are refusing. Offered as proof their suffering is handled, it quietly swaps the clinician's threshold for the patient's — but the threshold for what counts as an acceptable death is the patient's to set.

And even granting perfect palliative access arguendo: that is an argument to *fund palliation*, not to *prohibit the choice*. The two are opposite levers — one expands what is available, the other removes it — and a regime can run both at once, which is what the patient is owed. The objection welds 'improve care' to 'ban the exit' only by assuming the exit was always a mere workaround for inadequate care.

The residual, honestly: real palliative access is uneven, and some requests *are* under-treatment talking — a reason to screen for it (were palliative options offered and declined?) and to build access, not to delete the choice. Strip the empirical residual entirely and the bar still fails on the two structural points. The disagreement, as ever, relocates to whether sovereignty over one's own death exists.
responses.long:
Of the clinical objections, this is the one that aims at the paradigm case and lands closest. Where 'it's temporary' fails precisely on the intractable patient, palliative-sufficiency is built for them: it concedes the suffering is real and says care, fully resourced, can still meet it — up to and including sedation that carries the patient unconscious to death. It is the objection that most deserves to be met on the terminal, irremediable case rather than dodged toward easier ones. So meet it there, granting the clinical claim at full strength, and the inference still does not arrive.

Begin by disambiguating two claims the slogan runs together.

(A) Applied to a person — *for you, specifically, better palliation would relieve what is driving this.* A clinical claim about one case, which neither the objector nor this library adjudicates. Whether the palliation actually on offer is acceptable to this patient is the patient's determination; if it meets their need and they choose it, the library says nothing against that — it never tells anyone they should take the exit. The point is only that the answer is theirs.

(B) Applied as a categorical bar — *because palliation can manage suffering, the option must be unavailable to everyone.* This is the objection to the right, and it is the one that fails.

It fails because the clinical premise does not reach the conclusion without a bridge the objector never builds: the assumption that the request is *exhaustively* a request for relief from pain, so that any relief a clinician can supply renders it moot. Pull that assumption into the light and it is plainly false, in two directions.

First, and load-bearing: *manageable* is not *acceptable to this person*. The objection's strongest move — total or terminal sedation exists, therefore no suffering is unbearable-to-the-end — is the place it defeats itself, because what it describes is a patient rendered permanently unconscious until they die. For many who ask for the exit, that is not relief from the thing they fear; it *is* the thing they fear — the dissolution of the self before death, days or weeks of oblivion in a bed. To offer it as proof their suffering has been handled is to answer 'I do not want to die that way' with 'but you can be made not to know you are dying that way.' It installs the clinician's threshold for an acceptable death over the patient's own. And the threshold for what counts as an acceptable way to die is exactly the thing that is the patient's to set — not because their pain is worse than the objector imagines, but because it is their death. The objection has to assume the question of whose threshold governs is already settled in the clinician's favor. It is settled the other way.

Second: grant the empirical claim its best case — suppose flawless, universal palliative access, every dying person with impeccable hospice care. That is an argument to *fund palliation*. It is not an argument to *prohibit the exit*, because the two are not the same lever and not even adjacent ones. Funding palliation expands what is available to the patient; prohibiting the exit removes what is available to the patient. They answer different questions, and a regime can — and on the patient's behalf should — do both at once: maximal palliative access *and* the preserved choice. The objection's whole rhetorical force comes from welding the good half ('fix palliative care') to the bad half ('so ban the exit') and presenting the weld as a single act of conscience. Unwelded, the good half survives on its own and indicts no one's autonomy, and the bad half is left needing its own justification — which is the sovereignty question, not the palliation question. 'Improve care so the choice is unnecessary' only follows if the choice was never anything but a workaround for inadequate care, which is the conclusion the objection needed and never earned.

Now the empirical arm, routed deliberately so the core does not depend on it. The clinical premise — *adequate palliation can manage suffering to the end* — is contestable: a real fraction of dying patients have refractory symptoms that resist control, existential and total suffering that pharmacology does not reach, and access in the actual world is uneven, thinner for non-cancer trajectories, the rural, the uninsured. All of that strengthens the case against the bar. None of it is the spine. If palliation worked perfectly for everyone, the two structural points above would *still* defeat the categorical bar — the request can be grounded in sovereignty over one's mode of dying rather than in unrelieved pain, and funding is still not prohibition. The empirical shortfall is an amplifier; the argument is built to stand without it.

The residual, marked honestly. The objection is right about one thing, and it is not small: under-treatment is real, and some proportion of 'I want to die' is 'I am in pain that no one is treating,' which adequate palliation would dissolve. That is a genuine failure mode — and the correct response to it is to build the safeguard and the access, not to delete the choice. Crucially, this is a safeguard the regime can actually run: whether palliative options were offered, understood, and declined is *verifiable*, in a way that 'will this depression remit' is not — so the screening palliative-sufficiency motivates is more credible than the screening its sibling objections demand, not less. What does not sand away is the retreat: an objector can grant all of this and say that if palliation were truly universal and excellent, the only requests left would be sovereignty-driven, and that they deny sovereignty grounds the right. Correct — and that is where the disagreement belongs. The node wins the substitution point outright: care is something to provide, not a reason to forbid. The remainder relocates, as it always does, to whether a competent person holds authority over their own death.

objections.trigger: Legalize assisted dying and the law itself announces which lives society judges not worth sustaining — the disabled, the ill, the dependent. The option's mere availability is a message: that for people so situated, an exit is the intelligible, even fitting, response. Even if no one is pushed, the practice expresses that such lives are worth less, and that expressed judgment is a harm whatever any individual chooses.
objections.diagnosis: The argument slides from 'the option exists' to 'the institution asserts that disabled lives are worth less' — a step that holds only if availability-of-exit entails endorsement-of-exit-for-a-class, which is the same who-may-decide / which-lives-are-worth-living conflation the rebuttal isolates, now operating at the level of the institution rather than the individual.

responses.short: Pull the two claims apart. *The option carries a social meaning* — grant it. *That meaning is: your kind of life is worth less* — that does not follow. The right is exercised by an individual over their own death, for their own deferring reasons; it asserts nothing about any life's worth. The devaluing message is read into the option by the objector; the option predicates nothing. *Who may decide their own death* and *which lives are worth living* are different questions, and the expressivist fuses them. The real worry — structural pressure on the already-marginalized — is genuine, and it argues for safeguards, not for shutting the option for everyone.
responses.medium:
The expressivist objection is the strongest thing in the disability-rights case against assisted dying, and it deserves its steelman, not the coercion version it is often collapsed into. It does not claim that anyone is pushed. It claims that the practice *expresses* a judgment — that a society which makes an exit available for the ill and dependent has, by that availability, communicated that such lives are the kind for which an exit is fitting. The harm is in the message, and the message is said to be there whatever any individual chooses.

Concede the front half whole. Social practices do carry meanings beyond the intentions of the people inside them, and the disability-rights critique that marginalized lives are structurally devalued is owed a serious hearing, not a wave — and gets one, in the coercion node, with the empirical record attached. What does not follow is the content the objection assigns to the meaning. The option is exercised by an individual, over their own death, for their own deferring reasons; the right predicates nothing about the worth of disabled lives, or any lives. To get from *the exit is available* to *the institution judges your kind of life worth less*, the objector needs a bridging premise: that availability-of-exit entails endorsement-of-exit-for-a-class. That premise is the same conflation the whole rebuttal turns on — *who may decide their own death* read as *which lives are worth living* — now operating at the level of the institution rather than the individual. The option makes the first kind of claim and not the second. Reading the second into it is the objector's act, not the institution's.

The genuine residual — that *availability itself* fixes a social meaning regardless of any agent's exercise — is real, and named in the long form. But the structural-devaluation worry it rides on is an argument for safeguards: capacity assessment, anti-pressure screening, provision of real alternatives. It is not an argument for denying the competent agent authority over their own death.
responses.long:
This is the most serious objection the disability-rights tradition brings, and it has to be met on its strongest form, which is not the claim that disabled people will be pushed. That is the coercion objection, and it is answered elsewhere. The expressivist objection is subtler and, in a way, harder: it says that the *availability* of assisted dying is itself a communicative act. A society that makes an exit available for the ill, the disabled, the dependent has, in the very structure of the option, expressed a judgment about those lives — that for people so situated, ending is an intelligible, even fitting, response. The harm is not that anyone is coerced. The harm is in what the institution says by existing, and on the strongest version that meaning is fixed by the practice, present whether or not any particular person ever chooses the exit.

Concede the front half, and concede it without reservation, because it is true and because hedging it would be both dishonest and strategically foolish. Social practices do carry meanings that outrun the intentions of the individuals inside them; a law can say something a society did not sit down and decide to say. And the broader disability-rights claim — that the lives of disabled and dependent people are structurally devalued, materially and symbolically — is not a rhetorical flourish. It is a description of a real condition, and it is owed a serious hearing rather than a wave. It gets one: the coercion node concedes exactly this ground, and now carries the empirical record — documented cases where marginalization, not settled preference, shaped a request. None of that is in dispute here.

What is in dispute is the *content* the objection assigns to the institution's message. The option is exercised by an individual, over their own death, for their own deferring reasons. The right predicates nothing about the worth of disabled lives — nothing about the worth of any life. To travel from *an exit is available* to *the institution judges this class of life to be worth less*, the objection needs a bridge: the premise that making an option available endorses taking it, and endorses it for the class of people to whom it is most available. Name that premise and it is immediately recognizable. It is the conflation the entire rebuttal turns on — *who may decide their own death* heard as *which lives are worth living* — only now it operates at the level of the institution rather than the individual. A claim about who holds authority over their own death is categorically distinct from a claim about which lives are worth sustaining. The option makes the first. The second is read into it.

This is also where the charter guardrail becomes a structural feature rather than a constraint imposed from outside. The rebuttal must not, at any point, answer the expressivist by saying that disabled lives in fact carry less positive value, or that for some the exit is the rational choice — because that concession would make the accusation true, would supply exactly the devaluing content the objection alleges. The rebuttal rests nowhere near there. It rests on sovereignty: the option expresses, if it expresses anything, that a competent person holds authority over their own death and that the state declines to conscript their continuation. That is the whole of the institutional message the right actually carries, and it says nothing about worth. Resting the defense there is not a tactical choice; it is the only ground on which the defense does not concede the objection in the act of making it.

The residual is real and I will not sand it. The committed expressivist does not rest on individual exercise at all; the claim is that *availability itself* constitutes the message, that social meaning is a property of the institution, fixed independent of what any agent intends or chooses. On that view the distinction between the agent's act and the institution's expression is beside the point, because the meaning lives in the practice, not in the agent. Meet it directly. For *availability itself* to mean *this class is worth less*, the social meaning of an available option must be endorsement of its use — the institution must be read as recommending, for the class to whom the exit is most available, that they take it. But that is the bridging premise again, surfaced one level up: availability heard as endorsement, the option heard as a verdict on the user. The same distinction that defeats the individual version defeats the institutional one. An institution that licenses a competent agent's authority over their own death expresses non-conscription; to convert non-conscription into a verdict on the value of a class of lives requires precisely the availability-equals-endorsement premise the rebuttal has already pulled.

The expressivist can retreat further — to a thick account on which social meaning is constituted in ways no entailment captures, so that the practice can mean devaluation without any inference from availability to endorsement at all. But the retreat has a price, and it should be charged: the thicker and more agent-independent the social meaning is made, the less it can be steered by anything — including the safeguards, the anti-discrimination provisions, the public framing that a real regime builds precisely to fix the meaning the other way. A social meaning that floats entirely free of the institution's actual design and stated commitments is no longer a claim that this policy expresses devaluation; it is a claim that any availability would, which is just the original conflation asserted as an axiom. And the terminus, once the retreats are exhausted, is the same one the rest of the suite arrives at: does the social meaning the objector reads off the institution override a competent agent's authority over their own death? The expressivist's strongest honest answer is that it might — that the symbolic harm to a class could outweigh the sovereignty of the individual. That is a real position. It is not the position most pluralists hold when the question is put plainly, and it is not one the option's mere existence commits anyone to. The defense rests, finally, where it began: on the competent agent's authority over their own death, which the institution's expression of non-conscription respects and does not betray.

objections.trigger: Assisted dying violates the integrity of medicine. The physician's role is to heal; 'first, do no harm' is the oath's spine. A doctor who helps a patient die has crossed from healer to killer, corrupts the profession's character, and erodes the trust that makes medicine possible — the patient's confidence that the person at the bedside is unconditionally on the side of their life.
objections.diagnosis: The argument conflates the profession's self-conception with the patient's right: even granting that some physicians regard ending life as outside their role, that fact about medicine's self-image does not determine what authority a competent patient holds over their own death — yet the integrity claim renders a verdict on the second by asserting the first.

responses.short: Three moves, and only one is the patient's concern. *Medicine's telos forbids it* — contested, and the profession already withdraws life support at a refusal and sedates to unconsciousness under the same oath. *Participation corrupts the physician* — a claim about the doctor, answered by conscientious objection, which excuses the individual without abolishing the patient's option. *Trust erodes* — an empirical claim, owed evidence, and the regulated jurisdictions are the test bed, not a thought experiment. None of the three reaches the load-bearing point: the patient's authority over their own death does not depend on the profession's self-image. A physician may decline. The right is not the profession's to revoke.
responses.medium:
The integrity objection is three claims wearing one coat, and separating them dissolves most of its force. The first is about medicine's purpose: that healing is the telos, that 'do no harm' forbids hastening death, and that participation betrays what medicine is. But the telos of medicine is contested, not handed down fixed by one reading of *primum non nocere* — and the profession already does things that sit uneasily with the absolutist reading: it withdraws life-sustaining treatment at a competent refusal, it sedates to unconsciousness when nothing else relieves, it accepts under double effect that easing pain can foreseeably shorten life. Relieving suffering at a competent patient's sovereign request is not obviously outside a role that already contains those acts. (The objector's standard reply — that withdrawing and foreseeing are categorically unlike acting and intending — is a real line to contest, not a settled refutation; the analogy unsettles the telos claim without by itself closing it.)

The second claim is about the physician's character — that performing it corrupts the practitioner. Grant that some physicians experience it that way, and the answer is conscientious objection, not prohibition: the one who regards it as outside their role declines, and the patient's option survives intact. A claim about what this doctor may in good conscience do is not a claim about what that patient may decide.

The third claim is empirical: that trust in medicine erodes where physicians can also help patients die. That is owed evidence, not assertion — and it is testable, because regulated jurisdictions have run these frameworks for years. It is not a thought experiment to be won by intuition. Across the three, the load-bearing fact holds: the patient's authority over their own death is not contingent on the profession's self-conception. The residual — a physician-integrity absolutist who grounds the role in a non-negotiable duty to preserve life — is named in the long form, and routes to the same place: the patient's sovereignty is not the profession's to revoke.
responses.long:
The integrity objection has a respectable version and a sentimental one, and only the respectable version is worth the effort. The sentimental version is the slogan — first, do no harm, the doctor is a healer, killing is the opposite of healing — and it does not survive contact with what medicine already does. The respectable version is about trust: that the whole practice of medicine depends on the patient's confidence that the person at the bedside is unconditionally on the side of their continued life, and that this confidence cannot survive a profession that also, in some rooms, helps patients die. Take the respectable version; the sentimental one collapses into it once examined.

Begin with the telos, because the objection leans hardest on a fixed account of what medicine is for, and there is no such fixed account. The purpose of medicine is contested — relief of suffering, restoration of function, respect for the patient's own ends, the preservation of life — and these can conflict, and when they do, no single reading of primum non nocere adjudicates them by fiat. More concretely, the profession has already settled in practice that preservation of life is not lexically first. It withdraws life-sustaining treatment when a competent patient refuses it, knowing the patient will die. It administers sedation to unconsciousness when no lesser measure relieves, accepting that this may hasten death. It gives opioids at doses that foreseeably shorten life, under the doctrine of double effect. A role that already contains the deliberate withdrawal of life support at a patient's word, and sedation that forfeits consciousness for the remainder of a life, is not a role from which relieving suffering at a competent patient's sovereign request is self-evidently excluded.

The objector has a real reply here, and it should be stated rather than stepped around: withdrawing care is letting die, not killing, and double effect foresees death without intending it — so the acts the profession already performs are separated from assisted dying by exactly the act/omission and intention/foresight lines that integrity polices, and the analogy proves nothing. That reply is not nothing. But it does less than it claims. It must hold that the bright moral line falls precisely between foreseeing a death one's own hand hastens through sedation and intending a death one's own hand hastens through a prescription — a line under sustained pressure in the ethics literature, and one many clinicians do not experience as the difference between the permitted and the monstrous. The analogy does not need to collapse those distinctions to do its work; it needs only to show that the boundary of medicine is not the clean perimeter the integrity claim assumes, and that much it shows. The telos argument cannot carry a prohibition while the territory it polices is this contested.

The second move is the decisive one, because it shows the objection answering a question it was not asked. The integrity claim is about the profession's self-conception — what medicine takes itself to be, what this or that physician can in good conscience do. The patient's right is a different thing, and it does not depend on the profession's self-image. Suppose the integrity claim is granted in full: suppose ending life genuinely is, for many physicians, outside the role as they understand it. What follows is conscientious objection — the physician who cannot participate does not, and refers or declines — not the abolition of the patient's option. Individual conscience is honored without being made a veto over everyone else's authority. A claim about what this doctor may do becomes a claim about what that patient may decide only if the profession's self-understanding is allowed to define the limits of the patient's sovereignty — which is exactly the step that has to be earned and is instead assumed.

The third claim is the empirical one, and it has to be kept honest in both directions. Trust-erosion is not a conceptual truth; it is a prediction about how patients will relate to physicians under a permissive regime, and predictions are owed evidence. It is also, unlike most of this debate, testable — regulated jurisdictions have operated assisted-dying frameworks for years, and whether trust in those medical systems has measurably degraded is a question with an answer in the world rather than the armchair. The honest posture is to demand that evidence, not to assert the erosion and not to deny it; the rebuttal does not need the empirics to fall any particular way, only to insist they be produced rather than presumed. An objection that rests its weight on an untested empirical prediction has not yet earned the prohibition it demands.

The residual is the integrity absolutist, in two forms. The first grounds the physician's role in a non-negotiable duty to preserve life — a duty that does not bend to the patient's refusal, that makes participation a betrayal of medicine as such regardless of any individual conscience. Named plainly, this is the sanctity claim relocated into a professional register, and it meets the same terminus: a duty to preserve that overrides the competent patient's authority over their own death is not a fact about medicine, it is a contested value about the worth of continuation, asserted now in the profession's name — and the patient's sovereignty is not the profession's to revoke. The second form is subtler and more serious — that the profession's integrity is a public good, and its erosion harms not the objecting physician but every future patient who can no longer trust unconditionally. That is a real structure and deserves to be taken as one; but it is the trust-erosion claim again, and it carries that claim's burden. A public good whose damage is asserted and never measured cannot ground the removal of a competent person's authority over their own death. The patient's right does not wait on the profession's self-image to be settled, and it is not held hostage to an empirical harm the objection has so far only predicted. Conscientious objection protects the physician who cannot. Nothing in the integrity of medicine, honestly construed, requires that the patient be made to live.

objections.trigger: Legalize assisted dying for the terminally suffering and the category will not hold. This is not hypothetical; it is the record. Canada's MAID regime expanded from reasonably-foreseeable death to Track 2 within a few years. Belgium and the Netherlands authorize euthanasia for psychiatric suffering and have moved into dementia. The gate, once cut, widens: chronic illness, disability, the psychiatric, the demented who can no longer consent, the merely tired of life, and at the far end the quietly coerced — the cost-pressured, the burden-fearing, the institutionally nudged. Each expansion is defended in the vocabulary minted for the last. The slope is already greased. The principle you license does not stay where you put it.
keywords: where do you draw the line
objections.diagnosis: The slope equivocates on the gating criterion. The right defended is consent-gated sovereign exit; every feared endpoint sorts into one of two boxes. Either it is still a competent person choosing — which is the right working as designed, and the objector's real complaint is who qualifies, a line-drawing dispute inside consent, not the principle dissolving. Or it is a genuine consent-violation — which the sovereignty frame itself condemns as imposition in the right's costume, a different act on a different principle that the anti-imposition spine already prosecutes. The slide runs only if consent is first abandoned as the criterion, which the frame never does.

responses.short: Sort the feared endpoints before conceding the slide. The right defended is consent-gated sovereign exit — a competent person choosing their own death for their own deferring reasons. Every dreaded case lands in one of two boxes. Either it is *still a competent person choosing* — chronic illness, disability, a psychiatric patient who genuinely clears a capacity threshold — in which case it is the right working, and the quarrel is about *who counts as competent*, a line-drawing fight *inside* consent, not the principle dissolving. Or it is a *real consent-violation* — the demented with no prior directive, the coerced — in which case the sovereignty frame already condemns it: that is not an exercise of the right but an imposition wearing its clothes, and the library's own anti-imposition spine prosecutes it. The slope slides only if you first throw out consent as the criterion. The frame never does. *Abuse-of-X therefore prohibit-X* would close surgery, marriage, and contract law on identical logic.
responses.medium:
The headline slippery-slope is the version with teeth, because it does not gesture at hypotheticals — it points at the record. Canada moved from reasonably-foreseeable death to Track 2; the Benelux countries authorize euthanasia for psychiatric suffering. The gate widened. Take that as given. It is true, and pretending the expansions did not happen forfeits the argument's credibility for nothing.

What the objection equivocates on is the *criterion* doing the gating. The right being defended is consent-gated sovereign exit. Run every feared endpoint through that filter and it falls into one of two boxes. **Box (i):** still a competent person choosing — the disabled, the chronically ill, a psychiatric patient who genuinely meets a capacity threshold. That is the right operating as designed. The objector's actual quarrel here is *who qualifies as competent* — a hard, legitimate line-drawing dispute, but one conducted *inside* consent, not evidence that consent has stopped gating. **Box (ii):** a genuine consent-violation — the demented person with no prior directive, the person steered by cost or institutional pressure. The sovereignty frame does not slide *into* these; it *condemns* them. An imposition is not an exercise of the right; it is the right's costume pulled over a wrong, and the same anti-imposition spine that grounds the whole library prosecutes box (ii).

The slide therefore requires that you first abandon consent as the criterion. The frame never does — so box (i) is line-drawing and box (ii) is a different act on a different principle. The remedy the feared cases actually warrant is *tighter consent-verification and real material alternatives*, not *sealing the exit for the competent and uncoerced*. *Abuse-of-X entails prohibit-X* is a non-sequitur with no stopping point: surgery, marriage, guardianship, and contract are all abused, and we police the abuse rather than abolish the institution.

One premise the objection takes for free: that the no-right baseline is the safe one. It is not. Prohibition runs its own toll — protracted unrelieved agony, violent self-deliverance, lonely premature deaths timed to beat incapacity. The comparison is between two distributions of harm, not between harm and none; that denial of the free premise is defensive, not a recommendation of the act. The honest residual is named in the long form: the marginalization data suggests box-(ii) cases may be *patterned*, not rare — which indicts the adequacy of safeguards and is the objection's strongest card.
responses.long:
This is the slippery-slope objection in the form that should worry a defender, and the form that has to be met without flinching: not the hypothetical *imagine where this could lead*, but the empirical *look where it has already gone*. Canada legalized assisted dying for those whose death was reasonably foreseeable and, within a few years, opened Track 2 to those whose death was not. Belgium and the Netherlands authorize euthanasia for psychiatric suffering and have moved into the territory of dementia. The objection reads these as a single greased trajectory: the gate, once cut, does not hold its shape — it widens to chronic illness, to disability, to the psychiatric, to the demented who can no longer consent, to the merely tired of life, and at the far end to the quietly coerced, the cost-pressured, the burden-fearing, the institutionally nudged. Each expansion is justified in the vocabulary minted for the last. The principle, it says, does not stay where you put it.

Grant the record in full. The expansions are real, they are documented, and a defense that waves them away forfeits its own credibility to buy nothing. The honest question is not whether the category moved — it did — but what the movement *shows*.

What it does not show is that the gating criterion dissolved, and that is the equivocation the headline form runs on. The right under defense is consent-gated sovereign exit: a competent person, choosing their own death, for their own deferring reasons. Pass each feared endpoint through that filter and every one of them lands in one of two boxes.
