Box (i): the case is still a competent person choosing. A disabled person who qualifies, a chronically ill person, a psychiatric patient who genuinely clears a capacity threshold — these are not the principle sliding. They are the principle operating. What the objector is really contesting here is *who counts as competent to choose* — where the capacity line falls, how psychiatric suffering bears on decisional capacity, whether a given regime draws its thresholds too loosely. That is a serious and genuinely hard dispute. But it is a line-drawing dispute conducted *inside* consent, not a demonstration that consent has stopped gating. Disagreeing about where to set the threshold is not the same as showing there is no threshold. The advance-directive case is the hard edge of this box — a competent present self consenting on behalf of a future incompetent self — and it belongs here, as a question about how far prior consent reaches, not as proof the criterion failed.

Box (ii): the case is a genuine consent-violation. The demented person with no contemporaneous capacity and no prior directive; the person whose *choice* is the product of cost pressure, institutional steering, or fear of being a burden. Here the sovereignty frame does not slide *into* the abuse — it *condemns* it, on its own terms. An imposition is the precise opposite of an exercise of the right; it is the right's costume pulled over a wrong. The same anti-imposition spine that grounds every node in this library is the thing that prosecutes box (ii). It is not the bottom of *this* slope. It is a different act, on a different principle, that the defense was already against.

So the slide runs only if you first abandon consent as the criterion — and the frame never does. With consent held fixed, box (i) is line-drawing and box (ii) is a wrong the frame already names. The remedy the feared cases actually license is *tighter consent-verification and the provision of real alternatives* — not the sealing of the exit for the competent and uncoerced. *Abuse-of-X therefore prohibit-X* is a non-sequitur with no natural stopping point: surgery is abused, marriage is abused, contract and guardianship and power-of-attorney are all abused, and we respond by policing the abuse, not by abolishing the institution. Assisted dying earns no exception to that logic.

The objection also helps itself to a premise that should be charged for: that the status quo — no right — is the *safe* baseline, the neutral ground against which expansion is the only risk. It is not safe and it is not neutral. Prohibition runs its own toll: protracted agony that palliation cannot always reach, violent and traumatic self-deliverance, lonely deaths taken early and alone to beat the loss of the means to act at all. The real comparison is between two distributions of harm. And here the firewall is not a constraint imposed from outside the argument — it is load-bearing: the point is *not* that legalization lowers net suffering and the slope is therefore acceptable. That move would bless the destination, and the rebuttal blesses nothing. The point is strictly negative and strictly defensive — the objector does not get to assume prohibition is costless, because it is not. Denying the free premise is not the same as recommending the act, and the rebuttal stays on the near side of that line deliberately.

Now the residual, and it is the objection's strongest card, so it gets stated at full strength rather than sanded. The marginalization data — Ontario's own MAID Death Review findings that Track-2 recipients are drawn disproportionately from the most housing-unstable and lowest-resourced — suggests that box-(ii) cases may not be scattered aberrations but a *pattern* in who uses the expanded track. If that is right, it bites: it means consent-verification is failing not occasionally but structurally, for a population whose *choice* is shaped by a material desperation the state has done nothing to relieve. Concede the consequence honestly. If a regime cannot, in practice, distinguish a settled preference from that desperation, the case for restricting *that track* — raising its thresholds, or suspending it until the material alternatives exist — is strong. But notice that this concession is made *in the vocabulary of consent*, not against it. It does not show the principle slid; it shows a practice under-safeguarded. The patterned cases are box (ii) appearing at scale — impositions the frame condemns, indicting the implementation, not the criterion. The slope is greased only for the regime that lets consent go slack. Hold consent firm and there is no slope; there is a line, contested at its edges and betrayed in its worst cases, which is a reason to defend the line better, not to brick over the door.

objections.trigger: Grant the imposition-debt — that being forced into existence without consent creates a grievance owed compensation. The debtor is still the wrong party. You were imposed upon by your *parents*; they are the agents who acted. *Natalist society owes me a clean death* takes a debt incurred by procreators and bills it to the state, a third party that imposed nothing on you. Take it up with your parents. The state is a bystander you are dunning for someone else's liability — so it owes you nothing, and the claim-right to the means of dying, built on that debt, collapses with it.
keywords: take it up with your parents
objections.diagnosis: The objection equivocates between two questions and answers only the harmless one. *Who owes you the means to die?* is a positive-provision question, and on it the agent-mismatch genuinely bites — the procreator imposed, not the state. *Who may use force to prevent your exit?* is a negative-obstruction question, and on it the mismatch is irrelevant: the wrong of obstruction requires no prior debt. *Take it up with your parents* settles provision and leaves obstruction — the load-bearing charge, committed by the state now and in its own name — wholly untouched.

responses.short: Concede the whole debt structure and watch the right survive without it. Fork-2b grants the objection its premise: yes, if anyone *owes* you a death it is the parents who imposed existence, not the state. But the claim-right to be *provided* the means was only ever the *upgrade*. The load-bearing point is negative — whatever is true about who owes provision, no agent holds the standing to *conscript your continuation* by obstructing the exit. The state need not *owe* you a death to be barred from *preventing* one. And obstruction is something the state does *now, in its own name* — criminalizing presence at a death, foreclosing access to the means, punishing a willing assister — not a debt inherited from your parents. *Take it up with your parents* answers who *funds* the means and leaves the *obstruction* charge standing. The wrong of blocking a sovereign exit needs no creditor.
responses.medium:
The agent-mismatch is the sharpest move against the compensation route, and fork-2b answers it by refusing the route entirely — conceding the debt structure *arguendo* and showing the right does not need it.

Grant it whole: if existence is an imposition that incurs a debt, the debtor is the procreator, the agent who acted, not the state, which did nothing. *Take it up with your parents* is correct *as far as it reaches*. What it reaches is the *positive* question — who is obligated to *provide* you the means of dying. That was always compensation's particular job: to upgrade a liberty (the state may not stop you) into a claim-right (the state must furnish the means). Concede that the upgrade fails for want of a creditor with standing. The liberty does not fall with it.

Because the load-bearing charge in fork-2b is *negative*, and the negative wrong is independent of any debt. Actively obstructing a competent person's sovereign exit is wrong *as obstruction* — the interposition of coercive force between an agent and an act they could otherwise complete. The wrong of preventing requires no prior obligation to assist. The state need not *owe* you a death to be barred from *blocking* one. And blocking is not a liability passed down from your parents; it is something the state does in its own name, in the present tense — criminalizing presence at a death, foreclosing access to the means, threatening a willing private assister with prosecution. Your parents could, on the objection's own terms, incur a debt; they could never criminalize.

This is the anti-conscription move in compensation's clothing: the negative standing-denial — *no agent may conscript your continuation* — does the work the positive debt-frame was reaching for, and does it without a creditor. *Take it up with your parents* answers a question about provision and leaves the obstruction charge wholly untouched. The two questions never met. (Suffering enters here only to mark what obstruction *does* — it compels endurance of a sovereignly-rejected state — never to argue the exit is warranted.)
responses.long:
Fork-2b is the move that survives granting the objection everything it asks. The compensation route to a right to die runs through an imposition-debt: existence was forced on you without consent, that imposition is a wrong, the wrong incurs a debt, and the debt is discharged — among other things — by society owing you an unobstructed, even provisioned, exit. The agent-mismatch is the clean knife into that route. A debt has a debtor, and the debtor is whoever incurred it. You were imposed upon by your parents; they are the agents who performed the act the whole argument calls a wrong. *Natalist society owes me a death* takes a liability generated by procreators and bills it to the state, which imposed nothing on you. The state is a bystander dunned for someone else's debt. Take it up with your parents.

Concede it. Concede the entire compensation-and-debt structure *arguendo* — every link, including the agent-mismatch — because fork-2b's point is that the right needs none of it. The concession costs nothing it was relying on, and the discipline of making it is exactly what isolates the load-bearing claim.

Here is the distinction the objection collapses. *Take it up with your parents* is a decisive answer to a *positive* question: who bears the duty to *provide* you the means of dying — to furnish, fund, supply. That positive duty is precisely what compensation was introduced to manufacture. Its job was to upgrade a *liberty* (the state may not stop you exiting) into a *claim-right* (the state must actively put the means in your hands). Grant that the upgrade fails. Grant that no creditor with standing obligates the state to provide. The liberty is untouched, because the liberty never depended on the debt.

The wrong fork-2b actually charges is *negative*: not the state's failure to give you something, but the state's *active interposition of force* to stop you. Obstructing a competent person's sovereign exit is wrong as obstruction — and the wrong of preventing is categorically independent of any duty to assist. To wrong you by blocking, I need no prior obligation to help; I need only to put my coercive weight between you and an act you could otherwise complete. The state need not *owe* you a death to be barred from *preventing* one. And what makes this immune to *take it up with your parents* is its tense and its author: obstruction is not a debt inherited from the people who conceived you. It is something the state does *now*, *in its own name* — criminalizing presence at a death, foreclosing access to the means, threatening a willing private assister with prosecution. Your parents never held that power. They could, on the objection's own terms, incur a debt; they could never criminalize. So the charge that survives is one only the present-tense state can commit, and one the agent-mismatch cannot touch — because here there is no mismatch: the obstructing agent and the charged agent are the same agent.

The split has to be held against one push, because this is where it would leak. The objector says: criminalizing a *willing assister* is not the state forcing you to live — it is the state declining to *conscript* a third party into your death, which is itself a positive-provision question, so the agent-mismatch reaches it after all. No. Declining to conscript an *unwilling* assister would be non-provision — the state doing nothing, which fork-2b grants it may do. But the assister in question is *willing*; they are volunteering. Criminalizing them is not a refusal to compel the unwilling; it is the deployment of threatened punishment to *prevent a consensual act between competent adults*. The line is exact: non-provision is the state doing nothing; obstruction is the state deploying force to stop something. Fork-2b's charge attaches only to the second, and the second is not provision under any description.

This is the anti-conscription spine applied to compensation, and it is strong for the reason that spine is always strong: the negative standing-denial — *no agent holds the authority to conscript your continuation* — beats the positive frame it replaces. Keep it negative. The moment the argument reaches instead for *continuation causes suffering, so society must relieve it*, it has smuggled a suffering-warrant back in and drifted toward recommending the exit — and fork-2b was chosen precisely because it needs neither a suffering premise nor a debt premise. Suffering may enter only to characterize what obstruction *does*: it compels the continuation of a state the agent has sovereignly rejected, which is why blocking is an active harm and not a neutral non-act. It does not enter to argue that the exit is good or warranted. That door stays shut.

Two residuals, both real, neither sanded. First, the concession has a price the committed objector can name: fork-2b delivers the *liberty*, not the *claim-right*. For the person physically capable of self-administration, liberty is the whole of what they need — bar the state from obstructing and they can act. For the locked-in, the profoundly disabled, the person who *cannot* exit without provision, a liberty the state may not obstruct but need not satisfy is close to hollow; the upgrade fork-2b conceded away is exactly what that population requires. That is true, and fork-2b does not pretend to reach it. It establishes the floor — obstruction is wrong, no debt needed — and leaves the provision question, the upgrade to a claim-right, to a separate argument that would run on equal-access or non-discrimination grounds rather than on a suffering-warrant or a parental debt. Naming the limit is not a defeat; it is the boundary of what this particular move is for.

Second, and quickly: fork-2b concedes throughout that the exit is the *kind* of act sovereignty protects. An objector who denies that — who holds self-killing is not a self-regarding act the sovereignty frame covers at all — is not refuted here; that is a different objection, handled by the nodes that establish the act's protected status. Fork-2b is narrow on purpose. It defeats the agent-mismatch specifically, on the standing assumption the suite carries that a competent person's exit is sovereignty-protected, and it leaves the scope-of-sovereignty fight where it belongs. The mismatch was the whole of its target, and the mismatch does not survive contact with the negative charge.

objections.trigger: Make death a legal option and you hand the state an exit from its own obligations. Why fund housing, home care, disability support, mental-health services, when a lethal prescription is cheaper, faster, final? Under real deprivation the “choice” is a fiction: people ask to die because they cannot afford to live — because the supports that would have made life bearable were never funded. The right doesn’t liberate them; it launders their abandonment as autonomy. Look at the Canadian cases: applicants citing poverty, inadequate housing, untreated need. A society that offers its poor death before it offers them care has not expanded freedom. The door must stay shut until that society has discharged its duty to provide.
keywords: the state offers death not support
objections.diagnosis: The objection reads a choice shaped by social neglect as proof the right launders abandonment, when funding-provision and forbidding-the-exit are orthogonal levers — prohibition removes the option and leaves every deprivation standing — and the remedy for a deprivation-manufactured choice is to end the deprivation, not to conscript the deprived into continuation as restitution for having been failed.

responses.short: Two claims wear one coat. Deprivation manufactures some death-requests — concede it whole; underfunded care, absent housing, and abandoned disability provision do drive people toward an exit they would not choose under decent conditions, and the Canadian record shows it. Therefore close the option for everyone is the objection to the right, and it does not follow. The hinge is a swapped remedy. A choice produced by neglect is an indictment of the neglect — the corrective is to fund the provision that was withheld, not to delete the one door the deprived can still open. Funding-care and forbidding-the-exit are orthogonal levers: a regime can build housing, home care, and mental-health access and keep the exit, which is precisely what the deprived are owed — real alternatives to weigh against death, not one fewer option. Prohibition supplies neither the housing nor the care; it removes the exit and leaves every condition that manufactured the request exactly where it stood. And note what the bar actually proposes: because society failed to provide for you, you must be made to continue — abandonment answered by conscription. That is not a remedy for the wrong; it is a second wrong stacked on the first. Strip the empirical residual and the structure stands, and the disagreement relocates to whether anyone holds the authority to conscript a continuation.
responses.medium: The objection’s strength is that it points at something true and damning: there are real regimes where a lethal prescription is easier to obtain than a wheelchair ramp, and real applicants whose stated reason is poverty rather than pathology. Take that whole — it is the genuine residual, and the disability-rights critique that presses it is owed a serious hearing. The inference to prohibition still fails, on the structure of the wrong it names. Disambiguate first. Applied to a person — better provision would dissolve your reason to ask, so let us fix that before honoring the request — is, where true, exactly right; it is a reason to screen (were the supports offered? were they real?) and to build them, and the library does not adjudicate the individual case. Applied as a categorical bar — because deprivation can manufacture requests, the option must be closed to everyone, including the funded and well-supported who want it for reasons that have nothing to do with money — that is the objection to the right, and it is what fails. It fails because it welds two things that come apart. Funding the provision a person was denied and forbidding the exit are not the same lever in two grips; they are opposite motions. One expands what is available to weigh against death; the other removes an option and changes none of the deprivation. A regime can run both — fund the housing and the home care and keep the door — and that combination is what the deprived are actually owed: more to choose among, not less. The objection collapses ‘provide what was withheld’ into ‘prohibit the exit’ only by assuming the exit was never anything but a workaround for missing provision — which is the sovereignty question it has to win, not an observation it gets for free. And see the shape of what prohibition proposes. The premise is that society failed in its duty to provide; the conclusion is that the person it failed must be compelled to continue living anyway. Abandonment is to be answered by conscription — the very people the state under-served are the ones whose exit it closes, as if continued existence were the restitution they owe for having been failed. No party holds that authority. This is distinct from interpersonal coercion — a pressuring relative, a family deciding for the patient — which is acute and procedure-addressable; the wrong here is systemic, the state substituting an exit for a duty, and you do not cure a systemic deprivation by conscripting its victims. Strip the empirical residual to zero and the structural points stand untouched, and the disagreement relocates, as always, to whether a continuation can be conscripted at all.
responses.long: Begin where the objection is strongest, because it is strong. There are jurisdictions in which the path to an assisted death is shorter, better-resourced, and less encumbered than the path to housing, home care, or adequate disability support — and there are documented applicants whose decisive reason was material: a person who cannot secure accessible housing, who is exhausted by a benefits system that withholds what bare survival requires, who frames the request in the language of cost and burden rather than disease. The Canadian record has surfaced exactly such cases, and they are not edge anecdotes to be waved off; they are the live indictment. A society that has made dying easier to access than living has done something to be ashamed of. Concede all of it. The question is whether what follows is close the exit, and it is not. The objection runs two claims under one banner. The first — that deprivation manufactures some death-requests — is empirical and conceded whole. The second — that the option must therefore be prohibited for everyone — is the claim against the right, and it turns on a substituted remedy that does not survive inspection. A choice produced by neglect is, before anything else, an indictment of the neglect. The corrective that fits the wrong is to supply what was withheld: build the housing, fund the home care, restore the mental-health and disability provision whose absence did the manufacturing. Prohibiting the exit does none of that. It leaves the housing unbuilt, the care unfunded, the benefits as thin as they were — and removes, on top, the one door the deprived person could still open. The deprivation is untouched and the person has one fewer option; that is the entire effect of the bar. The move depends on treating two opposite levers as one. Funding provision expands what a person has to weigh against death; forbidding the exit contracts it. They are not the same act described twice; they pull in contrary directions, and a regime is free to do both at once — and owes both. What the deprived are actually owed is more to choose among: real alternatives, materially funded, set beside the exit so that the choice is genuine rather than cornered. ‘Fund what was withheld’ and ‘ban the exit’ are welded together only by an unstated premise — that the exit was never more than a workaround for missing provision, so that once provision arrives the exit has no further use. But that premise assumes the funded, well-supported person has no sovereign reason to want the door, which is the sovereignty question the objection is supposed to be answering, helped to itself for free. Two neighbors must be kept separate. This is not the palliative substitution, which offers clinical relief — manage the pain and the request dissolves — and fails because ‘manageable’ is not ‘acceptable to this person.’ Here the substituend is social provision, not symptom control, and the swap is performed by the state rather than the clinic. Nor is it interpersonal coercion — a pressuring heir, a relative deciding for the patient — which is acute, procedure-addressable, screenable by interviewing the person alone and imposing cooling-off. The wrong named here is systemic: an institution offering an exit in place of a duty it declined to discharge. Procedure does not reach it, because there is no single coercer in the room to screen out; the coercion is the ambient fact of having been under-provided. Which is exactly why the answer is provision, not prohibition — you do not repair a systemic deprivation by closing the exits of the people it deprived. Look squarely at what prohibition proposes here. Its premise is that society failed in its obligation to provide. Its conclusion is that the person society failed must be held to continued existence regardless. Abandonment answered by conscription: the under-served are precisely the cohort whose door is shut, as though continued living were the restitution they owe for having been failed — a second wrong laid over the first, and the more perverse for being addressed to the victim. No party holds the authority to conscript a continuation; the deprivation does not create that authority, and a state that produced the deprivation is the last claimant to it. The honest residual stands without flinching. Real provision is uneven and some requests are deprivation talking — which is a reason to screen for it, to ask whether genuine supports were offered and refused, and to bundle the option with funded alternatives so the choice is not manufactured by absence. It is not a reason to delete the choice, because deletion fixes none of the deprivation and conscripts the deprived. Imagine the limit case the objection needs: a just society, provision discharged in full — and a competent person who, supports and all, still wants the exit. The objection has nothing left to say to them; its entire force was borrowed from the deprivation it claimed to oppose. Strip that empirical residual to zero and the structure is unmoved, and the disagreement relocates where it always does — to whether anyone may conscript a continuation, the state included.

objections.trigger: Autonomy is the whole ground you stand on, and unbearable suffering knocks it out from under you. A person in agony isn’t choosing freely — the suffering is doing the choosing; it overwhelms deliberation, narrows the world to the pain, and makes the exit look like the only door. Call that a ‘request’ if you like, but it isn’t autonomous, because no one in that state is the free author of anything. So the autonomy your right rests on is precisely absent in the cases you invoke it for: the more unbearable the suffering, the less free the choice, until at the extreme there is no chooser left to respect — only suffering, asking to end itself.
keywords: no autonomy under that much suffering
not the author of the request
objections.diagnosis: The objection slides from ‘suffering pressures the choice’ to ‘suffering authors the choice, so no consent under it is valid’ — conflating a reason that motivates a competent agent with a coercer that overrides one, and never noticing that if duress voids the choice-to-exit it equally voids the imposed choice-to-continue and every consent-in-suffering with it, the objection’s own judgment among them.

responses.short: Distinguish the agent who is incompetent from the agent who is suffering; this objection is about the second and conflates it with the first. Grant everything that makes the case hard — full cognitive competence, no mental illness, a settled and durable preference. The claim is that the suffering itself vitiates the freedom of any choice made under it. It rests on a slide from ‘a reason that moves you’ to ‘a coercer that overrides you.’ A starving person’s choice to eat is driven by a powerful, unchosen pressure, and is not therefore unfree — it is reason responding to circumstance, which is what choosing under hard conditions is. Severe suffering is a weighty reason to want an exit; it is not an external will commandeering a competent one. And the principle devours itself if granted: if suffering vitiates the consent to leave, it equally vitiates the consent to stay — the default that suffering-under-prohibition imposes — and every decision made in pain, including the objector’s own confidence that the sufferer should continue. You cannot void one side of the ledger and keep the other. What remains, once the regress is seen, is the move itself: to declare a competent person’s suffering-driven choice ‘unfree’ is to transfer authority over their death to whoever gets to call it unfree. That is the conscription, wearing concern.
responses.medium: This is the deepest objection in the set, and the one most worth meeting on its own ground, because unlike the others it survives every empirical concession. Grant cognitive competence in full; grant no psychiatric disorder; grant a preference that has persisted and been examined; grant, even, a just society in which no deprivation is doing the manufacturing. The dying person still suffers — and the objection is that the suffering, by itself, makes the request unfree. It is not answered by capacity assessment, because the agent is stipulated competent. It has to be answered at the level it operates: the metaphysics of choosing under duress. The slide to expose is from a reason to a coercer. The objection treats ‘the suffering made them ask’ as if suffering were an external will that seized the controls — the way a gun to the head makes a signature meaningless. But severe suffering is not a second agent in the room; it is a circumstance the agent is responding to, and responding to a powerful circumstance with a reasoned preference is not the failure of autonomy but its exercise. The starving person who chooses to eat, the cornered animal that runs, the patient who refuses a treatment whose side-effects they will not bear — each acts under intense, unchosen pressure, and none is thereby rendered will-less. To make ‘driven by a strong reason’ equivalent to ‘coerced’ is to make almost no human choice autonomous, since we choose under pressures constantly. The objection needs suffering to be uniquely will-dissolving, and it never shows the uniqueness; it asserts it from the intensity. Then the symmetry, which is fatal if the premise is granted. Suppose suffering really does void the consent given under it. It does not void only the consent to leave. The person who is refused the exit and held to continued life is also choosing-under-suffering at every subsequent moment — their ongoing ‘consent’ to remain alive is extracted under the very duress the objection says invalidates consent. So the imposed continuation is no more autonomous than the requested exit; the premise condemns the default it was meant to protect. Worse, it condemns the objection itself, which is a judgment formed by people who are, like everyone, deciding under their own pressures. A principle that voids all consent-in-suffering voids the ground it stands on. You cannot apply it to the exit and suspend it for the continuation; either suffering is compatible with valid choice, or nothing chosen near suffering can be trusted, the prohibition included. And underneath both moves, the backstop. To pronounce a competent person’s suffering-driven choice ‘not really theirs’ is not a neutral finding; it is the transfer of authority over their death to whoever holds the pronouncing power — the clinician, the court, the bystander who is sure the pain is talking. The objection’s structure is the conscription move: it does not argue the person should stay, it argues the person is not the author of wanting to leave, and so installs someone else as the author of their staying. That is distinct from the incapacity case, where assessment really can find that a specific decision exceeds a specific person’s competence; here competence is conceded and the disqualification is done by the suffering alone — duress dressed as incapacity. Once the conflation, the symmetry, and the standing-transfer are on the table, the conceptual residue is spent, and the disagreement returns to its usual seat: whether anyone but the agent may rule a suffering agent’s choice unfree.
responses.long: This is the objection that does not dissolve under concession, which is why it sits at a different altitude from the rest. Hand it everything the empirical cases could want. The agent is cognitively competent — stipulate it, assessed and confirmed. No psychiatric disorder is authoring the wish; no depression, no transient crisis. The preference is durable: it has been held across time and survived examination. And the deprivation objections are answered — imagine the just society, every support funded, nothing manufactured by neglect. After all of that, the person is still dying and still in pain, and the objection makes its move: the suffering itself, not any defect of mind or circumstance, vitiates the autonomy of the request. There is nothing left to assess away. The claim is not empirical; it is a claim about what choosing is when it happens under duress, and it has to be met there. The first thing to expose is a slide between two pictures of how suffering relates to choice. In one, suffering is a reason — a powerful, unwelcome, unchosen feature of the situation that the agent weighs and responds to. In the other, suffering is a coercer — an external will that seizes the controls and acts through the body, the way a held gun makes a signature meaningless. The objection trades on the second picture while only earning the first. A reason, however overwhelming, leaves the agent the author of the response; a coercer replaces the agent. And almost everything we recognize as a hard human choice is the first kind. The starving person decides to eat; the exhausted patient declines another round of treatment whose burdens they will not carry; the person in grief reorders their life around a loss they did not choose. Each is driven by intense, unchosen pressure, and we do not say their will was absent — we say they chose under hard conditions, which is most of what choosing ever is. To collapse ‘moved by a strong reason’ into ‘coerced’ is to evacuate autonomy from the human case wholesale. The objection survives only by insisting suffering is uniquely will-dissolving, and that uniqueness is asserted from the sheer intensity of the pain, never argued. Intensity is not authorship. There is a more sophisticated form: not that suffering overrides deliberation, but that it distorts the values the deliberation runs on — that the person in agony is not weighing their settled commitments but a temporarily warped scale, so the choice, though competent, is not authentic. Grant the distinction between competent and authentic and the objection still over-reaches, because it proves far too much. Every strong affective state shapes the scale we weigh on — love, fear, exhaustion, hope. We do not hold that decisions made under their influence belong to someone else; we hold that the standing agent made them. And the test the objection needs — a value reordered by suffering is inauthentic — cannot distinguish the case it wants to bar from the cases it must allow, including the long-considered conclusion of someone who has lived with their condition for years and reordered nothing in haste. Authenticity, pressed this hard, becomes a license to overrule any choice an observer finds out of character, which is not a safeguard but a veto. The decisive answer is the symmetry, and it is fatal the moment the premise is taken seriously. Suppose suffering genuinely voids the consent given under it. Then notice what it voids besides the exit. The person refused the door and held to continued life consents to nothing freely either — every further moment of their staying is a choice made under the same suffering, extracted under the same duress the objection says destroys valid consent. The imposed continuation is therefore no more autonomous than the requested exit; the premise indicts the default it was deployed to defend. And it does not stop there. The judgment that the sufferer should continue is itself formed under pressure — by clinicians, families, bystanders, all deciding as humans decide, in the grip of their own fears and hopes. A principle that nullifies all consent-in-suffering nullifies the ground beneath the objection. There is no consistent place to stand that voids the choice-to-leave while honoring the choice-to-stay: either suffering and valid choice are compatible — in which case the request can be autonomous — or nothing decided in the vicinity of suffering can be trusted, prohibition first among the casualties. Beneath both moves lies the backstop that makes the objection’s politics visible. To declare a competent person’s suffering-driven choice ‘not really theirs’ is not a neutral observation about agency; it is a transfer of authority over that person’s death to whoever holds the power to pronounce it unfree — the clinician who is sure the pain is talking, the court, the relative who cannot bear the request. The objection does not, in the end, argue that the person should remain alive. It argues that the person is not the author of wanting to leave, and in doing so it installs someone else as the author of their remaining. The structure is the conscription move itself, dressed as solicitude. This is precisely where it parts from the incapacity objection, which is a different and more honest claim: there, assessment can genuinely find that a particular decision outruns a particular person’s competence, and gating the exercise on that assessment is the right answer. Here competence is conceded from the start, and the disqualification is performed by the suffering alone — duress costumed as incapacity, applied to an agent everyone agrees is competent. The honest residual is narrow and belongs to the neighbor, not here. Some conditions really do author the desire rather than merely accompany it — but those are conditions, diagnosable and assessable, and they live in the capacity objection where gating does the work; they are not ‘suffering as such.’ For the case this node defends — the competent, undeluded, persistently suffering agent — the objection has no purchase that does not also strip autonomy from the whole of human choosing or saw off the branch it sits on. What is left, when the conflation of reason with coercer is exposed, the symmetry is granted its consequences, and the standing-transfer is named, is the question that was always underneath: not whether the choice is free, but who, other than the one whose death it is, gets to declare it unfree. The library’s answer is no one.

objections.trigger: Set aside whether the suffering will lift — grant that it won't, or that no one can know. Death is still the one choice you cannot revise. Every other decision leaves a standing self who can reconsider, adapt, be surprised by a future they couldn't foresee; death forecloses the chooser along with the choice. When one branch is irreversible and the other is not, and you are deciding under uncertainty, the precautionary structure of the situation — not optimism, not the prognosis — favors the branch that keeps every option open. Even a competent, settled agent should defer to that asymmetry, and a regime that lets the irreversible branch be taken has failed to respect it. Better the error you can still walk back.
